hints: Focus on what is removed from pyruvate in the link reaction - a molecule of carbon dioxide and hydrogen atoms - so think about what type of helper molecules are needed to carry hydrogen and a 2-carbon group away.
Recall that one hydrogen-carrying coenzyme becomes reduced NAD, and the other combines with the remaining acetyl group to make acetyl coenzyme A.
walkthrough:
What the Link Reaction Does**
Pyruvate is a 3-carbon molecule. In the matrix it is oxidised - hydrogen is removed - and decarboxylated - carbon dioxide is removed - leaving a 2-carbon acetyl group. That chemistry needs carriers to pick up what is removed.

Matching the Two Carriers**
The hydrogen is picked up by NAD to form reduced NAD. The acetyl group is picked up by coenzyme A to form acetyl coenzyme A, which then enters the Krebs cycle. Those are the two coenzymes.
Final answer: NAD and coenzyme A.

hints: Start by reading both axes in Fig. 9.1 and check the starting point - both curves start at 100% activity at 0 minutes, then follow each line separately to 10 minutes.
Compare the steepness and final position of the two curves to decide if activity falls in both cases and whether the higher $H_2O_2$ concentration causes a faster or larger fall.
Pick one time point, for example 5 or 10 minutes, and read off a pair of percentage activity values with units of $H_2O_2$ concentration to prove the comparison.
walkthrough:
Describe Each Trend Separately**
Both lines fall from 100% at 0 minutes. That tells you exposure to $H_2O_2$ reduces activity over time in both treatments. It is not activation, it is loss of activity.

Compare Like With Like**
The lower curve is always the $0.5 \times 10^{-3} mol dm^{-3}$ treatment. It falls more steeply, especially in the first 3 minutes to about 68%, while the $0.1 \times 10^{-3} mol dm^{-3}$ treatment only falls to about 90% at 3 minutes. By 10 minutes the values are about 40% versus about 71%.

Link Pattern to Biology**
A larger fall with more $H_2O_2$ means $H_2O_2$ acts as an inhibitor of this Krebs cycle enzyme. Always quote paired data with units to earn the data mark.

Final answer: Enzyme activity decreases over time at both $H_2O_2$ concentrations; decrease is greater / faster at higher $H_2O_2$ concentration, so $H_2O_2$ inhibits the enzyme. e.g. at 10 min activity is ~71% at $0.1 \times 10^{-3} mol dm^{-3}$ but ~40% at $0.5 \times 10^{-3} mol dm^{-3}$.

hints: Start from the energy already released by electrons moving along the inner membrane - think where that energy goes and what it can move across the membrane.
Remember the mitochondrion has two compartments separated by the inner membrane, so pumping creates a difference in concentration that stores energy.
Think how protons get back to the matrix and what enzyme lets them through to couple that movement to making ATP from ADP and Pi.
Finish by recalling what must happen to electrons at the end of the chain to keep flow going and why oxygen is essential for this.
walkthrough:
Build the Proton Gradient**
As electrons pass from carrier to carrier, they lose energy. That energy is used to pump protons ($H^+$) from the matrix into the intermembrane space. This creates a high concentration of protons outside and a low concentration inside - an electrochemical proton gradient.

Use the Gradient to Make ATP**
The inner membrane is impermeable to protons except through ATP synthase. Protons diffuse down their gradient through ATP synthase. This is chemiosmosis. The flow turns the enzyme and provides energy to join ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi) to make ATP.

Keep Electrons Flowing With Oxygen**
At the end of the chain electrons must be removed or the chain blocks. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor. It combines with electrons and protons to form water. Without this, proton pumping and ATP synthesis would stop.

Final answer: Energy released pumps $H^+$ into the intermembrane space forming a proton gradient; $H^+$ diffuse back through ATP synthase by chemiosmosis driving ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi; oxygen accepts electrons + $H^+$ to form water.

hints: Think about what happens during fast running when muscles need ATP faster than oxygen can be supplied - what alternative pathway follows glycolysis.
Recall what product builds up in muscle and blood when pyruvate cannot enter the Krebs cycle and must be converted to something else.
Think why extra oxygen is still needed after stopping - what processes need ATP and oxygen to remove that product by oxidation or rebuilding glucose.
walkthrough:
Why Lactate Forms During Exercise**
In fast running, oxygen supply cannot meet ATP demand. Muscle still runs glycolysis but pyruvate cannot all go through aerobic respiration, so it is reduced to lactate in anaerobic respiration. Lactate accumulates.

Why Oxygen Is Needed Afterwards**
Lactate is not waste to be left. It must be removed. That needs oxygen for aerobic respiration to provide extra ATP through the electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation.

How the Debt Is Repaid**
The extra ATP and oxygen allow lactate to be oxidised to $CO_2$ and water, or converted back to glucose and glycogen in the liver. Until that is complete, oxygen consumption stays above resting level. This is repaying the oxygen debt.

Final answer: During exercise anaerobic respiration produces lactate; after exercise oxygen is needed to oxidise lactate to $CO_2$ and water via Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation to make ATP; ATP is also used to convert lactate to glucose / glycogen in the liver, repaying the oxygen debt.
